t.bahla fort@23.0,57.3:
Bahla Fort rises above the oasis like a mountain made of mud. Its massive walls and towers of adobe and stone, built on a rocky outcrop in the plain below the Hajar mountains, were the stronghold of the Banu Nebhan, a tribe that dominated the region from roughly the twelfth to the fifteenth century. Around the fort, the old town of Bahla is enclosed by a wall that runs for kilometres across the oasis, and the date palms and fields inside are watered by aflaj, ancient irrigation channels that carry water from underground sources and springs. UNESCO listed the fort in 1987, and after years of restoration, it is open to visitors.

Bahla has long had a reputation for magic and the supernatural, and many Omanis still associate the town with jinn and sorcery. More tangibly, it is known for its pottery, made by hand from local clay, and you can visit workshops in the town. A short ride away, Jabrin Castle, built in the seventeenth century, is a beautiful fortified palace with painted ceilings and carved woodwork, and the aflaj irrigation systems of Oman are listed by UNESCO in their own right.

The riding in the interior of Oman is excellent. The main roads are good, with smooth tarmac and little traffic, and the scenery of rocky mountains, desert plains and green oases is stunning. To the north, the road up to Jebel Shams, the highest mountain in Oman, climbs through steep hairpins to a viewpoint over a deep canyon, sometimes called the Grand Canyon of Arabia. The road to Jebel Akhdar, the Green Mountain, is steep and has a police checkpoint at the bottom, where they may insist on four-wheel drive vehicles. The heat in summer is extreme, often over forty-five degrees, so ride early in the morning and rest in the afternoon.

Bahla, with over fifty thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Nizwa, about twenty-four kilometres away, is a larger town with a famous fort and a souq. On Fridays, the Nizwa livestock market is a lively spectacle. Try shuwa, lamb or goat marinated with spices and slow-cooked underground, and drink kahwa, Omani coffee flavoured with cardamom, served with dates.
t.falaj daris@23.0,57.5:
Water has always been the measure of wealth in the Omani interior, and at Nizwa it arrives through a channel that has been flowing for centuries. Falaj Daris is the largest of the aflaj, the traditional irrigation systems of Oman, and it carries water from underground sources in the foothills of the Jebel Akhdar to the date gardens and fields of Nizwa. The system works by gravity, with tunnels and open channels sometimes running for kilometres, and the water is shared among farmers according to an ancient system of time-based rights, managed by a local official. Falaj Daris is one of five aflaj inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2006, recognising a technology that may go back two thousand years or more.

Nizwa itself was once the capital of Oman and remains one of its most important historic towns. Its massive round fort, built in the seventeenth century, dominates the centre, and the old souq, with its silver, pottery and spice shops, is famous for the Friday livestock market, where goats and cattle are auctioned in a lively circle. The Jebel Akhdar, the Green Mountain, rises behind the town, with terraced villages, rose gardens and pomegranate orchards on its high plateau.

The riding here is spectacular. The main road from Muscat to Nizwa is a modern dual carriageway, fast but dull, but the roads into the mountains are another story. The climb up the Jebel Akhdar is a steep, winding road with tight hairpins, and access is controlled by a police checkpoint, where only four-wheel-drive vehicles are normally allowed through; check current rules for motorcycles before you go. The road west toward Bahla and Jabrin passes forts and oases, and the road to Jebel Shams, Oman's highest mountain, climbs to the edge of a deep canyon, with the final stretch unpaved. Summer temperatures are extreme, regularly over forty degrees, so the cooler months from October to April are the time to ride.

Nizwa is a city of over seventy thousand people, with plenty of fuel stations, restaurants and hotels. Omani food includes shuwa, slow-cooked marinated meat, and halwa, a sticky sweet served with strong coffee flavoured with cardamom. Walk along the falaj where it emerges into the date gardens, listen to the water, and feel the coolness it brings. In this dry land, it is a small miracle.
t.falaj al muyasser@23.4,57.5:
Water decides everything in Oman's interior, and the falaj is how people have managed it for well over a thousand years, by some accounts much longer. A falaj is a channel that brings water from a mountain spring, a wadi or an underground source, sometimes through tunnels dug by hand, and divides it among the farms of a village according to a strict timetable of shares. Falaj al-Muyassar in Rustaq is one of five aflaj inscribed by UNESCO in 2006 as examples of this system, which still keeps date palm gardens green at the edge of the desert.

Stand by the channel and watch the water run, clear and fast, under the palms. Traditionally, an official, the arif, oversaw the distribution, with time measured by the sun by day and the stars by night, and shares of water could be bought, sold and inherited like land. Mosques, washing places and the gardens all had their place in the order of the flow. In the heat of the afternoon, the shaded gardens along the falaj feel like an oasis in the literal sense.

Rustaq is one of the historic towns of Oman, once a capital, and its fort, restored and open to visitors, is a vast mud-brick and stone structure with towers looking out over the plain to the mountains. Nearby, the hot spring of Ain al-Kasfa flows out at a high temperature and is channelled into bathing pools and the gardens. Behind the town rise the Western Hajar mountains, the highest in eastern Arabia, rugged, bare and cut by deep wadis.

The riding is excellent and needs respect. The main roads from the Batinah coast to Rustaq are wide and well surfaced, with long fast curves across the gravel plains, and traffic is light outside the towns. Beyond, gravel tracks lead into the mountains, most famously the route through Wadi Bani Awf over to the other side of the Jebel Akhdar massif, steep, rough and spectacular, normally driven in four-wheel drive and serious terrain for a heavy bike. Heat is the main enemy: from May to September, temperatures are extreme, and riding should be limited to early mornings. The winter months are glorious.

Rustaq, a town of tens of thousands, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and is only five kilometres away. Carry plenty of water when you leave it. Omani hospitality means you may be offered coffee spiced with cardamom and a plate of dates, and accepting is part of the pleasure.
t.hili 2@24.3,55.8:
Jebel Hafit rises out of the flat desert like a wall of grey limestone, and at its foot lie some of the oldest tombs in the Arabian Peninsula. Hili 2 is part of the archaeological park on the edge of Al Ain, in Abu Dhabi emirate, where beehive-shaped stone tombs were built around five thousand years ago, in what archaeologists call the Umm an-Nar period. The round towers of neatly cut stone, some with carved animals and human figures on the doorways, held collective burials, and the place is also home to remains of a Bronze Age settlement and ancient irrigation channels called falaj. The tombs, together with the oases and the hill, are part of the UNESCO listing of the cultural sites of Al Ain, inscribed in 2011.

The oasis is the second story. Al Ain means the spring, and for millennia the date palm groves have been watered by underground channels bringing water from the hills. Walking through the old plantations, among mud-brick walls and shaded lanes, is a cool relief from the surrounding heat, and you can see how settled life in the desert depended on this clever engineering.

The ride that most bikers want is the road up Jebel Hafit. About twelve kilometres long, with more than sixty bends, it climbs to over twelve hundred metres at a viewing platform, with smooth asphalt, wide curves and dramatic views over Al Ain and the desert to Oman. It is popular with drivers and cyclists, especially at weekends and sunset, so go early or on a weekday, and watch for sand on the corners. At the top there is a hotel and a small parking area.

Al Ain has about half a million people and Al Buraymī, across the Omani border, about seventy-four thousand, so fuel and food are easy. The border crossing at Buraimi requires visas and insurance, and rules for motorcycles change, so check them first. Summers are punishingly hot, with temperatures above forty-five degrees, so the season runs from November to March, when mornings are cool and clear. Drink water constantly, wear a light jacket for the speed, and finish with a cup of Arabic coffee and fresh dates.
t.archaeological sites of bat@23.3,56.7:
There is a ridge in the Omani interior where stone beehive towers still stand in a line against the sky, and they are about five thousand years old. The Bat area, near the oasis town of Ibri on the edge of the Hajar mountains, holds some of the best preserved remains of the Bronze Age in the Arabian peninsula, along with the nearby sites of Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn. The beehive tombs were built in the third millennium BC, in the so-called Umm an-Nar period, from stacked, dressed stones, and the settlement towers beside them watched over a landscape of wadis and date palms.

The people who built them were part of a trading world. Oman was then known to the Sumerians as Magan, a source of copper that was shipped to Mesopotamia and the Indus valley, and the settlements along the mountains grew rich in the process. Standing among the tombs at dusk, with the stones glowing and the mountains beyond, it is not hard to see why they chose these ridges. The area is also tied to the falaj system, the ancient channels that bring water from mountain springs to the fields, and which still operate in many oases. UNESCO listed the sites in 1988.

The riding here is mostly straight, hot and spacious. The road from Nizwa towards Ibri crosses desert plains with the Hajar range as a constant backdrop, and the light at the beginning and end of the day is magnificent. Summer temperatures can pass forty-five degrees, and riding in the middle of the day is both foolish and tiring, so plan for the winter months, from November to March, when the days are warm and the nights cool. Sand can blow across the road, and camels sometimes appear without warning.

Ibri is a substantial town of about a hundred thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and many small cafes, and the last place to make sure that you have water and a full tank. Beyond the main road, services are thin, and the tracks to the sites are rough in places. Drink a lot, wear light, long sleeves, and accept an offer of dates and coffee if one comes.
t.jebel hafit desert park@24.1,55.8:
For riders in the Gulf, there is a road that people talk about with real affection. Jebel Hafit, a long, rocky ridge that rises out of the flat gravel plain on the border between the United Arab Emirates and Oman, is about 1,240 metres high, and a smooth tarmac road snakes up its eastern flank in a long series of hairpins and bends to the top, a distance of about eleven kilometres. At the summit, a hotel and a viewing terrace look out over the oasis city of Al Ain, with the desert stretching away to the horizon, and at dusk the lights come on below like a field of stars. Motorcyclists and cyclists come here in the cooler months, usually early in the morning or at sunset, and the road is one of the best in the country.

The mountain is also an archaeological site. On the ridges and slopes are the Hafit tombs, hundreds of beehive-shaped stone burials from about 5,000 years ago, some of the oldest monuments in the Arabian Peninsula, and they give their name to the Hafit period of the early Bronze Age. They form part of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain, inscribed as World Heritage in 2011, along with the Hili Archaeological Park, the oases and the Bidaa Bint Saud site. The mountain is a fold of limestone, rich in fossils, and the rock layers tilt steeply, so the geology is clear. At the foot of the mountain, the Green Mubazzarah park has hot springs and chalets.

The riding is short but excellent. The road is very well surfaced, with sharp hairpins, steady gradients and barriers along the edge, and in the cool season you can run up and down it more than once, though speed limits are enforced and cameras and police are common. Stay within the rules, since the penalties in the UAE can be severe. The best time is from November to March, when temperatures are mild, and in summer the heat, often above forty-five degrees, makes riding in the afternoon dangerous. Sand can blow across the road after wind, and in rare cases rain makes the surface very slippery.

Al Ain, about fifteen kilometres away, has plenty of fuel, restaurants and hotels, and the border town of Al Buraimi, in Oman, is a short ride beyond. Dress modestly in towns, carry your documents, and bring water.
t.hili north tomb a@24.3,55.8:
The Hili tombs sit in the oasis landscape where Oman meets the United Arab Emirates, and the border here is a line on a map rather than a barrier on the ground. The Omani town of Buraimi and the Emirati city of Al Ain run into each other, with palms, fields and low sandy hills, and these stone tombs are among the oldest standing monuments in the region. They are circular towers of carefully cut limestone, built around 2500 BC in what archaeologists call the Umm an-Nar period, and they were used as communal graves.

The people who built them were farmers and traders. They mined copper in the nearby mountains and exported it by sea to Mesopotamia, and they developed irrigation channels known as falaj, underground tunnels that bring water from the hills to the oasis by gravity. The falaj system still waters date palms here and is part of the reason the cultural sites of Al Ain were listed by UNESCO in 2011. Carvings of human figures and animals survive on some of the stones, and they feel remarkably alive after four and a half thousand years.

Riding here is oasis riding: flat tarmac, roundabouts, date plantations behind mud-brick walls, and sudden stretches of desert. Summer is brutally hot, with temperatures above forty-five degrees, so ride in the early morning, or choose the cooler months from November to March. Be careful of sand drifting onto the road, and watch for speed cameras, which are common. Crossing the border between Oman and the UAE requires proper paperwork, visas and vehicle documents, so check what applies to your passport and vehicle before arriving.

Buraimi, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafes, and Al Ain, on the other side of the border, has a wide range of services. Visit the old fort in Buraimi for a sense of the region's later history. Carry plenty of water, wear sunscreen and respect the site by not climbing on the stones. Dates and strong cardamom coffee are the traditional welcome, and a handful of fresh dates is a fine reward.
t.hili north tomb b@24.3,55.8:
Jebel Hafit is the mountain that dominates the skyline here, a long, jagged limestone ridge rising abruptly from the desert plain on the border between Oman and the Emirates. Its slopes are littered with beehive-shaped stone tombs, built about five thousand years ago, among the oldest of their kind in the Arabian Peninsula. Hili North Tomb B belongs to the same oasis landscape as the better-known Hili sites and is a short ride from Buraimi, with the mountain filling the horizon to the south.

Hafit is a motorcyclist's mountain. The road to the summit, on the Emirati side, climbs about eleven kilometres with more than sixty bends and hairpins, a well-surfaced, wide road that has become one of the most famous driving routes in the Gulf. It rises to about 1,200 metres, where a hotel and viewpoint look out over the desert and the lights of Al Ain at night. Because it is popular with local riders, it can be crowded on weekend evenings, with some fast and some foolish driving, so take it steadily.

The Jebel Hafit Desert Park, another stop on the same ride, protects the landscape around the foot of the mountain, with gazelles, Arabian oryx and desert birds. The rocks themselves are full of fossils, with ancient marine creatures recorded in the limestone, showing that this desert was once under a shallow sea. The light is best at sunrise and sunset, when the ridge turns copper and the shadows deepen.

Summer heat is severe, with midday temperatures that can top forty-five degrees, and the road surface can become very hot, so ride early or late, and carry plenty of water. Winter is the best season, with clear skies and pleasant temperatures. Buraimi has fuel and basic food, and Al Ain, a few kilometres on the other side of the border, has a larger choice of workshops, hotels and cafes. Border crossings need the right documents, so check requirements well ahead of time. Take a camera and some patience, because the views repay a slow pace.
t.hili oasis@24.3,55.8:
Hili sits on the border of two countries, and for a rider the line is the first thing worth knowing. Al Buraymi on the Omani side and Al Ain on the Emirati side share a single oasis belt at the foot of Jebel Hafit, and the border runs through the town in a way that has been softened by the long shared history of the tribes who live on either side. Take your passport, check what your insurance and rental papers say about crossing, and expect to be waved through slowly rather than quickly.

The oasis is the older story. Date palms planted in rows, shaded by their own fronds, grow beside narrow irrigation channels called falaj, which carry water from underground sources and from the mountains over distances that make you stop and think about the effort. This system is thousands of years old, and the Hili area has Bronze Age tombs and a settlement site that shows people have farmed here since before writing. The graves are round, built of neat stone, and sit in a park where you can walk around them for little or no money.

Riding around Hili is not about corners. The roads are wide and straight, with roundabouts in neat rings and wide verges planted with trees, and in the evening the heat leaves them slowly. The only real hill in sight is Jebel Hafit, a hard limestone ridge standing alone out of the plain and looking larger than its height suggests. In July and August the air is brutal, easily above forty degrees by midday, so do your riding at dawn or after the sun has gone. Between November and March the weather is mild and the light is good, which is when the place makes sense.

Fuel is plentiful and cheap, as the Gulf generally is, and Al Buraymi with its roughly seventy thousand people offers everything: shops, cafés, petrol stations, a restored fort. Carry water on the bike all the time and top it up at every stop. Dates and Arabic coffee are offered as a courtesy in many places, and a small cup of the latter, with cardamom, is a perfectly good reason to sit in the shade for ten minutes.
t.al qattara oasis@24.3,55.8:
Qattara is one of the old oases of Al Ain, a cluster of palm gardens that once fed a handful of mudbrick houses and towers. The area has been inhabited for thousands of years, and the whole group of oases is recognised by UNESCO for the way people have managed water in a place where it hardly rains. At Qattara you can still see the old layout: shaded lanes between walls, small farm plots under the palms, and a fort that was built to protect the wells and the people who relied on them.

The fort was restored and today holds a small arts centre and craft displays, and the market nearby sells dates, spices and local goods in a quieter way than the big city souqs. It is a place to walk slowly. The air inside the gardens is noticeably cooler than outside, and the sound of water in the falaj, a bubbling thread of irrigation, is a better soundtrack than most.

Jebel Hafit is the other half of the story, rising on the near horizon. It is the highest peak in the emirate of Abu Dhabi at over twelve hundred metres, a long ridge of folded limestone with fossils in its sides, and the road to the top is a rider's treat. It twists up in a long series of hairpins and bends for about a dozen kilometres, with fine tarmac, good barriers and views over the plain that get bigger with every turn. At the top there is a hotel with a terrace, and on a clear evening you can watch the lights of two countries come on. Beehive-shaped tombs of the Hafit period, some five thousand years old, dot the lower slopes, and you can see them from the road.

Go early, because the summer sun makes the plain unbearable and the wind at the summit can be gusty. Weekends bring cars and sightseers, and on a Friday evening the top road gets busy, so try for a weekday. Water is essential, and fuel is easy in Al Buraymi and Al Ain, both only a few kilometres away. In winter the weather is wonderful, and desert nights get a chill that surprises first-time visitors.
t.cultural sites of al ain@24.1,55.8:
Al Ain is called the Garden City, and the name is earned. It is a large, spread-out oasis town at the foot of Jebel Hafit, close to the border with Oman, and its green roundabouts, date plantations and tree-lined avenues look like a deliberate argument against the desert. The UNESCO cultural sites here bundle together a handful of places: the Hafit tombs, the Hili archaeological park, the Bidaa bint Saud area, and the oases of the town itself. The theme is human life in a dry land, over a very long time.

Start with the oldest layer. The beehive tombs on the slopes of Jebel Hafit date back some five thousand years, and the large round tombs at Hili belong to the Umm an-Nar culture of the Bronze Age, built from carefully cut stone with carved relief on some entrances. They sit in open ground and you can walk right up to them. Much later come the mudbrick forts, such as the Al Jahili Fort, built in the nineteenth century, which houses a museum and an exhibition on early desert exploration. The father of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Zayed, was born in the Al Ain area, and the story of the state is told in the local museums with some pride.

For riding, Al Ain gives you wide roads, orderly traffic and the great hairpin road up Jebel Hafit, which is one of the best known in the Gulf and a little tricky when it is crowded. Speed cameras are plentiful and fines are real, so keep to the limit. Summer heat is intense, over forty degrees most days, and the best time to be out is between late October and March, ideally early in the morning.

Fuel is everywhere. Al Ain has well over half a million people if you count the whole city, with shops, cafés and malls in air-conditioned comfort. Water and shade are the real essentials, so top up your bottle and take a break among the palms, where the temperature can feel ten degrees lower. Coffee is served in small cups, dates are offered as a sign of welcome, and you should accept both without fuss.
t.saigachy beleuli@44.6,57.2:
This is a place where the map offers few names and even fewer roads. What I can describe is the landscape, and it is one of the most austere in the world: pale, stony ground, scattered tufts of saltwort and wormwood, and a horizon as flat as a table, broken only by the edge of the plateau where it drops in chalk cliffs known locally as chinks.

The name Saigachy comes from the saiga, the strange, big-nosed antelope that once roamed the steppes in millions. It is a creature that looks half ancient, with a bulbous snout that filters dust and warms the winter air. The herds migrate across the Ustyurt, and their numbers fell disastrously in the 1990s and again in 2015, when disease killed hundreds of thousands in a few weeks. Conservation efforts have helped some populations recover. Goitered gazelles, wild asses called kulan, and wolves also live on the plateau, and eagles hunt over the open ground.

For riders, the plateau is a dream and a danger at the same time. The main roads that cross it, linking Kazakhstan and Karakalpakstan, are long tarmac lines with enormous distances between settlements, and the side tracks are sand and gravel that can swallow a bike. Summer temperatures are brutal, often above forty degrees, and winters bring ice and fierce winds. Spring, when the steppe briefly flowers, and early autumn are the best times.

There are no reliable services off the main road. Carry fuel for far more than you expect to need, water for days, tools, a satellite messenger if possible, and a local contact who knows the tracks. The nearest real towns are a long way off, and the ones that exist are small. Border formalities in this region can be complicated, so check what permits are needed. The landscape reward is silence, and a sky that seems to go on forever.
t.al naqfa ridge@24.2,55.8:
Al Ain is the Garden City of the UAE, an oasis town where date plantations are watered by falaj channels, ancient underground canals that have carried mountain water for more than three thousand years, and the shade of the palms is a relief after the desert glare. UNESCO inscribed the city's cultural sites in 2011, including the Bronze Age tombs at Hili, the oases and the sites at Bidaa Bint Saud, a stony ridge with traces of ancient settlement and rock art.

The ridge is part of the great spine of the Hajar foothills, a bare landscape of limestone and gravel with isolated hills rising from the plain. The nearest and most famous is Jebel Hafeet, which stands about 1,250 metres above sea level and looks down on the city. Archaeologists have found beehive tombs there that date back to around 3000 BC. The mountain also holds a hot spring, and the summit has views across the border into Oman. The Al Jahili Fort in town was built in the 1890s and houses a gallery about the explorer Wilfred Thesiger.

For motorcyclists, Jebel Hafeet is the draw. The road to the summit climbs about eleven kilometres through many hairpins, carved into the mountain with wide, smooth tarmac and good barriers, and it has become a favourite for riders in the Gulf. The corners are open and the surface is excellent, but the road can be busy on weekends, when cars and cyclists crowd the hairpins. Winds are strong near the top, and the air is noticeably cooler. Summer heat is intense, so ride early or in winter.

Practically, Al Ain has fuel stations, supermarkets and many cafes, and the old oasis is a pleasant place for a stroll. If you plan to cross into Oman at Al Buraimi, take your passport and vehicle papers and check the entry rules in advance, because insurance and customs requirements apply. Bring plenty of water and avoid the midday sun. A coffee under the palms, followed by a late-afternoon climb up the mountain, is a very fine way to spend a day.
t.nizwa@22.9,57.5:
Nizwá was the capital of Oman for centuries, and it still feels like the heart of the interior. About seventy thousand people live in this oasis city, at the foot of the Hajar Mountains, among date palms watered by falaj channels, the ancient irrigation systems that carry water from the hills by gravity, some of which have been in use for more than a thousand years. UNESCO has recognised the aflaj of Oman for their importance.

The fortress dominates the skyline. Built in the seventeenth century under the Imam Sultan bin Saif Al Ya'rubi, it has a huge round tower, with thick walls and cunning defences, and the view from the top over the palm groves, the souq and the mosque dome is superb. The souq next door sells dates, spices, pottery and silver, including the curved daggers called khanjars that are part of traditional dress, and the smell of frankincense and coffee drifts through the alleys. On Friday mornings, the livestock market draws farmers with goats and cattle, in a lively auction that has been going on for generations.

Then there is the halwa, a sweet, sticky, spiced confection made with sugar, ghee, rose water and nuts, stirred for hours in huge copper pots. It is the town's best known treat, and shops sell it in boxes, with a cup of cardamom coffee.

For riders, Nizwá is a gateway to the mountains. Jebel Akhdar, the Green Mountain, rises north of the town to over two thousand metres, with terraced villages growing pomegranates and roses, and the road up is steep and winding. A police checkpoint at the foot is known to restrict access to certain vehicles, so check the current rules before you plan. Jebel Shams, Oman's highest peak at nearly three thousand metres, lies to the west and has a gorge often called the Grand Canyon of Arabia.

Heat is the main challenge, with summer temperatures well over forty degrees, so ride in the cooler months from October to March, and start early. Dust and sand can drift across the road, and animals, especially camels and goats, wander freely.

Fuel and services are plentiful in Nizwá, with many stations, and Bahla, about twenty-four kilometres away, has more. Fill up here before heading to the mountains, as services are limited, and carry plenty of water.

Go in the late afternoon, when the fort glows gold and the heat eases.
t.troitsko pechorsk@62.7,56.2:
Troitsko-Pechorsk sits on the upper Pechora River, which here is a clear, strong stream, with gravel banks and forested hills on both sides, and it is the gateway to the largest stretch of primeval forest in Europe. The Virgin Komi Forests, protected in the Yugyd Va National Park and the Pechora-Ilych Reserve, cover an area bigger than many countries, and in 1995 they became the first natural site in Russia to be placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. They include spruce, fir, larch and birch taiga, mountain tundra, bogs and a chain of the northern Ural peaks, including Mount Narodnaya, the highest in the Urals at around 1,895 metres.

The town is small, with about eight thousand people, a scatter of wooden houses and Soviet blocks, and a long street along the river. It exists mostly as a service centre for the surrounding district, with a sawmill, a few shops and a local museum devoted to the region, and it has the feel of a place at the edge of the settled world. The name joins the Trinity to the river. Beyond it, the roads get quieter, and the next sizeable town is a long way off.

For a rider, it is a long way from anywhere, and that is the point. The road from Syktyvkar is long, and the surface varies, with some good modern stretches and some rough ones. The forest closes in on both sides, and for hours you may see only timber trucks. Further east, the roads turn to gravel and dirt, and conditions change quickly after rain, so a dual-sport bike and a patient mind are the right tools. In summer, mosquitoes and midges are severe, and a head net is worth packing. Weather can turn cold and wet at any time, and snow falls early in autumn. The best season is late June to early September.

Practicalities matter here. There are petrol stations in town, but supplies thin out fast beyond it, so fill up and carry some extra if you plan to go further. Shops stock basics, and there are guest houses and a simple hotel. If you want to visit the national park, you will need to arrange permits and advice from the park offices.

Walk to the river in the evening, and look upstream. The water comes from mountains you cannot see, through forest no one has cut.
t.yaksha@61.8,56.9:
Yaksha is a name on the map of the Komi Republic, a scatter of forest settlement on the upper reaches of the Pechora, in a district where the population is counted in handfuls per hundred square kilometres. The nearest proper town is Troitsko-Pechorsk, some way to the north, and between the two lies taiga: spruce, fir and pine in long dark ranks, broken by bogs, rivers and the occasional logging clearing.

The geography is the story. The Pechora rises in the northern Urals and runs a long way north before it turns to the Arctic, and in its upper course it is fast, clear and full of fish, with grayling, taimen and salmon in the colder reaches. The valley is lined with old river terraces and low hills, with limestone outcrops in places, and in autumn the larch turns a pale, burning yellow against the dark spruce. This is Komi country, and the Komi have lived off this forest for centuries, hunting, fishing, gathering berries and mushrooms, and herding reindeer to the north. A fair number of the older settlements have shrunk since the Soviet years, when logging camps and forced-labour settlements dotted the region, and what remains is often a handful of houses, a store and a school.

Riding here is serious. The roads are mostly forestry tracks and rough local routes, gravel and dirt, with long stretches of washboard and mud, and rivers crossed by simple bridges or fords. A dual-sport bike is the right tool, and you should expect to go slowly. There is almost no traffic, so a breakdown can mean a long wait, and mobile coverage is patchy or absent. In summer, mosquitoes and midges are ferocious, and a head net is a basic necessity. Weather can turn cold and wet in any month, and snow can arrive in September. The best window is late June to early September, though July is the buggy peak.

Fuel and supplies are the real challenge. Tell someone where you are going, and keep a paper map.

Spend a little time just listening. The only sounds are likely to be wind, water, and the odd bird.
t.puerto piramides@-42.6,-64.3:
Puerto Pirámides is a village of a few hundred people on the shore of the Golfo Nuevo, on the Valdés Peninsula in Patagonia, and it is the best place on the continent to meet a whale. From roughly June to December, southern right whales come into the sheltered bay to mate and give birth, and tour boats set out from the beach to watch them. The peninsula, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the richest wildlife areas in Argentina, and the village is its small and very friendly gateway. The name comes from the pyramid-shaped cliffs near the shore.

The ride from Puerto Madryn is about a hundred kilometres across flat, windswept steppe. Most of the main road is paved, with long straights and gentle bends, and the riding is easy, though crosswinds can be strong and the road is shared with tourist buses in summer. Beyond the village, the roads that circle the peninsula are mostly gravel, with loose stones, soft patches and long distances between settlements, so the going is slower and needs more care. The best months for wildlife are September to November, when the whales are most active, and the weather is cool and bright.

An unusual feature of the village is the huge tidal range. At low tide the sea retreats far across the beach, and boats are launched by tractors that drag them out over the sand. It is a curious sight, and the beach is a good place to sit with a coffee and watch the activity. A few cafes, restaurants and guesthouses cater to visitors, and there is a small shop, though prices are higher than on the mainland. Fuel may be limited, so fill the tank in Puerto Madryn, and carry some extra if you plan to tour the peninsula.

The peninsula is rich in animals. Sea lions and elephant seals lounge on the beaches, Magellanic penguins nest in colonies, and guanacos, rheas and Patagonian hares roam the steppe. At the northern tip, in March and April, killer whales sometimes charge up the shingle to catch sea lion pups, a behaviour seen almost nowhere else. There is a park fee for the reserve, and rules about distance from the animals, which are strictly enforced. Spend time on the beach, watch the tide, and you may see a whale breach in the distance.
t.falaj al katmeen@22.9,57.7:
At the foot of the Hajar mountains, near the old town of Birkat al Mouz between Izki and Nizwa, the Falaj al Khatmeen is one of five Omani irrigation systems listed by UNESCO as the Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman. A falaj is a channel that brings water from a spring or an underground source, sometimes kilometres away, to villages and date gardens, and this one has been running for centuries. What makes the aflaj remarkable is the system of sharing: the water is divided among the owners of shares by time, traditionally measured by the shadow of a sundial by day and the movement of the stars by night, and the rules are managed by the community with great precision. Walking along the narrow stone channel, with fish darting in the clear water and the shade of the palms overhead, you feel the coolness that comes from water in the desert.

Birkat al Mouz has a ruined old quarter of mud-brick houses climbing the slopes behind the gardens, and a restored fort. The mountains behind rise steeply to the Jebel Akhdar, the green mountain, a high plateau with terraced gardens of roses, pomegranates and walnuts, famous for the rose water that is distilled in spring. The road up to the plateau begins nearby and climbs in a long series of steep bends; there is a police checkpoint at the bottom that controls access to the plateau, so check the current rules for vehicles before you go.

Riding in Oman is a pleasure in the cooler months, from October to April. The roads are excellent, smooth and well signposted, traffic is generally disciplined, and the mountain scenery is spectacular, with bare rock in shades of brown, grey and purple. In summer, temperatures are brutal, and riding in the middle of the day is unwise. Watch for speed cameras, which are very common, and for camels and goats on the road outside towns.

Nizwa, about fourteen kilometres away, is the big town of the interior, with its massive round fort, the souk and the Friday livestock market, an extraordinary sight early in the morning. It has fuel, hotels and restaurants, as does Izki. Try Omani halwa, a sticky sweet flavoured with rose water and saffron, served with bitter cardamom coffee and dates, a ritual of hospitality you will encounter everywhere.
t.bidaa bint saud@24.4,55.7:
Jebel Hafit rises out of the flat gravel desert near Al Ain like a lizard's back, a bare, folded limestone ridge about twelve hundred metres high that marks the border between the United Arab Emirates and Oman. It is the best-known landmark in the area, and the scatter of ancient sites around it tells the story of the people who lived here. On the lower slopes are about five thousand years old beehive-shaped stone tombs, the first examples of a type of grave that is now named after the mountain, and the Hafit period is a recognised phase of Bronze Age archaeology in south-east Arabia.

Bidaa Bint Saud is part of the group of cultural sites around Al Ain that UNESCO listed in 2011, together with Hili, the Hafit tombs and the oases of the district. The area is known for aflaj, the underground and surface irrigation channels that carry water from the mountains to the date palm gardens, an engineering system with a history of thousands of years. The oases of Al Ain are still green, shady and cool, with date palms, mud-brick walls and shaded paths, and they feel a long way from the glass towers of Dubai.

For riders, the great attraction is the Jebel Hafit mountain road, a ribbon of smooth asphalt that climbs from the plain to a summit viewpoint with many hairpin bends, wide open bends and big views over the desert. It is one of the best-known motorcycle roads in the Gulf, and it gets crowded in the evenings and at weekends, so be careful with speed and watch for sand on the surface, especially after wind. In summer, the heat is extreme, often above forty-five degrees, so the best months are November to March, and the best hours are early morning and sunset.

Al Ain, across the border from the town of Al Buraymi in Oman, has fuel, which is cheap by European standards, and food of every kind. Al Jahili Fort, built in the 1890s, is worth a visit, and the camel market gives a glimpse of an older way of life. If you cross the border to Oman, have your documents and insurance in order, because the checks can be strict, and bring a pocketful of patience as well as water.
t.aflaj irrigation systems of oman@23.0,57:
Nizwa lies at the foot of the Hajar mountains in the interior of Oman, and its date groves exist because of a method of bringing water that is older than the town. The aflaj, plural of falaj, are channels that carry water by gravity from mountain springs or underground sources to fields and villages, sometimes for many kilometres. UNESCO listed a group of five in 2006, among them Falaj Daris, which feeds Nizwa and is one of the largest in the country. Some aflaj are believed to be very old, perhaps thousands of years, and they are still in use, with the water divided among families by time, measured by sundials in the daytime and by the stars at night.

You can follow the channel from where it emerges and watch the water slip along the stone-lined course, past mosques and little gardens, until it splits into small channels to feed date palms, pomegranates, lime trees and alfalfa. The coolness and shade of the oasis, after the dry hills, is like entering another climate. It is a sociable system, too: an official oversees the distribution, and arguments are settled by custom.

In Nizwa itself you should visit the great round tower of the fort, built in the seventeenth century under the Ya'ruba imam Sultan bin Saif, with views over the palms and the old market. On Friday mornings a livestock market is held nearby, a lively scene of goats, cattle and loud bargaining. The halwa shops, selling Oman's sticky sweet, are a local tradition, and the old souq is the place for silver and daggers.

The road from Muscat is a pleasure: about a hundred and sixty kilometres of good highway through the gravel plains and past bare, jagged mountains, with reasonable traffic and a few speed cameras. The Jebel Akhdar road nearby is a steep climb with a police checkpoint and, for safety, a restriction to four-wheel-drive vehicles, so check before you set out. Summer is extremely hot, with temperatures often over forty-five, so choose the cooler months from October to March. Nizwa, with over seventy thousand people, has plenty of fuel, cafes and hotels.
t.falaj al malki@22.7,57.8:
The Falaj Al-Malki is one of the irrigation channels that UNESCO listed in 2006 as part of the aflaj of Oman, and it lies near Izki, in the valley below the great wall of Jebel Akhdar. Izki is an old oasis town with palm groves and a ruined mud-brick quarter, strategically placed at the Sumail Gap, the natural pass that has linked the coast and the interior for thousands of years. Caravans, armies and traders all passed here, and the town has always had its share of tribal rivalries and politics.

The falaj works by a simple principle: water collected from an underground source or a spring flows by gravity along a gently sloping channel, often partly underground, to the village. There are three kinds, distinguished by their source: the daudi type, which taps deep underground water through a tunnel; the ghaili, which draws from a wadi; and the ayni, which comes from a spring. Maintaining them is community work, and water rights are shared by time rather than volume, with each family having a measured slot. A system like this takes real cooperation, and it has endured because it works.

Riding here is wide-open and dramatic. Highway 15 from Muscat runs across the plain to Izki, with the bare, sharp ridges of the Hajar to the north and sandy desert to the south, and the long, empty distances mean the wind and the heat dominate. Midsummer is very hot, with temperatures above forty degrees, so ride early and stop often, drinking plenty of water. The cooler months from late October are much more comfortable, and in winter the nights are fresh.

Izki has about thirty-six thousand people, with petrol stations, small restaurants and shops. Nizwa, over thirty kilometres away, has more choice. A meal of shuwa, meat slow-cooked in an underground oven, is a classic Omani dish, usually prepared for festivals, though you may find something similar in local restaurants. Rest in the shade near the falaj if you can; the sound of running water in a dry country is a quiet but powerful experience, and the oasis can be surprisingly cool even in the heat of the day.
t.al ain wildlife park tombs@24.2,55.7:
Jebel Hafit rises out of the flat desert at the edge of Al Ain like a long, pale whale, and on its lower slopes sit some of the oldest buildings in the United Arab Emirates. These are beehive tombs, circular cairns of stacked stone, built around five thousand years ago in the early Bronze Age, which give their name to the Hafit period of Arabian prehistory. Dozens of them survive on the ridges and foothills, and the ones near the wildlife park are easy to reach, standing in the open on a spur of rock with the town on one side and the dry mountain on the other.

The tombs are part of the cultural sites of Al Ain, listed by UNESCO in 2011 together with the old oasis, the Hili archaeological park and the Bida Bint Saud area. The oasis around the town is still green with date palms, watered by the ancient falaj channels, and the old mud-brick fort of Al Jahili, built in the 1890s, is where Sheikh Zayed, the founder of the UAE, was born. Al Ain is called the garden city, and it has a quieter, shadier feel than the coastal cities.

For riders, Jebel Hafit has a special attraction. A road of about twelve kilometres climbs the mountain in a long series of hairpins and bends, widely known for smooth surfacing and an endless run of bends, and rises to a plateau of over a thousand metres with a view across the desert to the Omani mountains. At the top there is a hotel and a viewpoint, and the sunset from here is superb. The road is popular with cyclists and drivers, especially on weekends, and there are speed cameras, so keep to the limit. Sand can blow onto the road, and the evenings can be busy.

Heat is the main issue. From June to September temperatures are extreme, with highs often over forty-five degrees, so ride in the early morning or after sunset. From November to March it is warm and pleasant, with clear skies, and this is the best time to visit. Fuel is cheap and plentiful in Al Ain, and cafes and restaurants stay open late. Across the border, Buraimi in Oman is only a few kilometres away, with the old forts and the market, though the border crossing needs your papers and the right insurance for the vehicle.
t.hili archaeological park@24.3,55.8:
Five thousand years ago, people on the edge of the Arabian desert built beehive-shaped stone tombs on the ridge of Jebel Hafit, and the oasis town below them has been continuously lived in ever since. Hili is part of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain, and the park holds a grave of the Umm an-Nar culture, the Hili Grand Tomb, built of precisely cut stone with carved reliefs of human and animal figures on its entrance. Traces of a Bronze Age settlement, with circular towers and wells, add to the picture of a society that had learned to farm in a dry land through the falaj, the underground channels that bring water from the mountains.

The park is a pleasant landscape of date palms, pale sand and gardens, with a modest ticket and clear signs. The Omani border town of Buraimi lies almost next door, and the two places form one oasis. The old forts, shaded souks and mud-brick walls feel unhurried, and in the afternoon the date palms offer welcome shade.

The great attraction for riders is Jebel Hafit itself. A well-surfaced road climbs about eleven kilometres to the summit at around twelve hundred metres, with a long series of switchbacks and sweeping bends and with views over the desert plain, and it is a favourite of motorcyclists in the Emirates. Early morning or evening is best, when the heat is lower and the stone glows. In summer the temperatures are extreme, with highs above forty-five degrees, so the cooler months, from November to March, are the time to ride. Watch for sand across the road, and for speed cameras, which are frequent and strictly enforced across the United Arab Emirates.

Al Ain has every service, including fuel stations on every main road, large malls and restaurants, and the nearby town of Al Buraymī in Oman does too. The border between the two countries has changed over the years, so carry passport, vehicle papers and insurance cover that is valid in both countries if you plan to cross. Fuel is cheap, and tea and dates are offered as a matter of course. Wear sunscreen and a hat, and carry water even for short visits, since the park has little shade among the tombs.
t.rumailah site@24.3,55.8:
Jebel Hafit rises out of the flat desert on the border between Oman and the United Arab Emirates like a long, pale whale, and the ground around its foot is dotted with small stone domes. These are the Hafit tombs, built about five thousand years ago, and they give their name to an entire period of the Bronze Age in the region. Rumailah is one of the clusters on the Omani side, a short distance from the town of Al Buraimi, and from the site you can look across the border and see the ridge standing up in the haze.

The tombs are beehive-shaped, made from carefully piled limestone slabs, and each one probably held several burials. They were built on the lower slopes and ridges, in places visible from the plain, and archaeologists think they marked territory and ancestry as much as death. Nobody is sure who the builders were or where they lived, though the oases below must have supported them, and pottery and beads from the tombs show links with Mesopotamia and Iran. Some tombs have been restored and a few are still in surprisingly good shape.

Riding here is easy, hot and flat. Good tarmac runs through Al Buraimi, a town of about seventy thousand, where you will find fuel at many stations, cafes and shops, and the roads leading to the mountain are wide and quiet. Summer temperatures reach more than forty-five degrees and make midday riding miserable, so go between November and March, or start at dawn. Take water, sun protection and a hat, as there is no shade at the tombs.

Remember that the Omani and Emirati towns of Buraimi and Al Ain run into each other, and there is a border crossing in between, so keep your passport and vehicle papers with you. Rules for crossing with a foreign motorbike can be complicated, so check in advance. After dark, the ridge turns purple, and a cold drink in a Buraimi cafe is a good way to end the day.
t.west ridge hafit tombs@24.2,55.7:
The road up Jebel Hafit is one of the best-known motorcycle climbs in the Gulf, and it is easy to understand why. It runs for about twelve kilometres, with dozens of well-surfaced bends and hairpins that wind up the flank of the mountain to a summit plateau at roughly 1,200 metres, and from there you can see the whole of Al Ain spread out below and the desert running into the haze. In a country of motorways and flat horizons, it is a gift.

West Ridge sits on the other side of this story. Along the ridges below the road, small stone beehive tombs have stood for five thousand years, built in the Early Bronze Age and now grouped in lines along the crest. Hundreds survive on the mountain, and they were among the reasons why Al Ain's cultural sites, including Hili and the oases, were inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. There is something peculiar about riding up through a modern road and seeing, on the skyline, a row of graves older than the pyramids at Giza.

Hafit is a limestone mountain, folded and layered, with fossil shells in the rock, and the slopes are bare and golden. Early in the morning, the air is cool and clean, and the light is soft on the cliffs. By midday in summer, the rock is too hot to touch, so go at dawn or in the evening, and avoid the midday heat. In the winter, there is sometimes mist in the early hours.

The base of the mountain is on the edge of Al Ain, a city of garden avenues and date palms, so fuel and food are easy to find before you go up, but there is little at the top apart from a hotel, so fill the tank and carry water. Watch for cyclists and for drivers who treat the road as a racetrack, and for sand on the corners after windy days. Parking at the summit viewing points is easy.
t.al muwaiji oasis@24.2,55.7:
Al Ain is called the Garden City, and the Al Muwaiji area gives you the reason. Inside a ring of mud-brick walls, date palms grow thick and tall, shading small plots of vegetables, citrus trees and fodder, watered by the old irrigation channels called aflaj. These are underground and open channels that bring water from the hills, some of them used for around three thousand years, and the system is still in use. UNESCO included the oases of Al Ain in its 2011 listing of the area's cultural sites, alongside the Bronze Age tombs of Hafit and Hili.

Walking into the oasis, you leave the heat and traffic behind in about thirty seconds. The air is cooler and damper and smells of earth, dates and wet leaves, and the light comes through the fronds in patches. The lanes are narrow and the walls are high, and this is one of those places that feel secret even though it sits in the middle of a city. Visit early, before the day warms up, and expect a very quiet atmosphere.

Close by stands the Al Muwaiji Fort, a square mud-brick building from the twentieth century. It was the home of the ruling family and is known as the birthplace of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the founding president of the United Arab Emirates, who was born here in 1918. The fort is now a museum, and you can see the old rooms, and learn how the family lived before oil changed everything.

For riding, the surrounding city is a grid of wide, well-kept roads with lots of roundabouts, and traffic is moderate. The population is large, and Al Ain has fuel stations on every main road, plenty of cafes, and a range of places to stay. Summer is hot beyond comfort, with temperatures above forty-five degrees, so the cooler season, from November to March, is the one to choose. Dress modestly when visiting heritage sites, and ask before taking photographs of people.
t.birkat al mouz@22.9,57.7:
Birkat al Mouz sits at the foot of Jebel Akhdar, between the date palms of the plain and the grey wall of the mountain, and it is one of the places in Oman where the old water system is easiest to understand. The village is known for its falaj, a channel that carries water from the mountain through tunnels and open ditches to the fields, and the system here is part of the group of aflaj recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage. Water was shared out by the hour, using sundials by day and the stars by night, and a person called the wakil kept the accounts. The system is more than a thousand years old, and it still works, feeding groves of date palms, bananas, mango trees and small plots of vegetables.

Above the new village stand the ruins of the old one, a labyrinth of mud-brick houses, towers and alleys, abandoned as people moved to modern houses, and slowly melting back into the earth. It is worth walking through, if you can do so safely, for the sense of how people lived. The date plantation gives shade and a green relief from the desert heat.

The ride to Birkat al Mouz is straightforward. The main highway from Muscat runs towards Nizwa through the gap in the mountains, and a side road leads to the village. The surface is good, the bends are gentle, and traffic is light. Heat is the main factor, since summer temperatures can pass forty-five degrees, and the best time to ride is from October to March, when the days are warm and the air is clear. Start early, carry water, and wear light, loose layers over your protective gear.

Izki, about ten kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and cafés, and Nizwa, the old capital and market town, is a short ride farther, with everything you need. The area is famous for dates, and you can buy fresh ones in season, along with halwa, a sweet, sticky dessert flavoured with rosewater and nuts. Take a cup of qahwa, the local cardamom coffee, if it is offered, and accept it with the right hand. It is a polite way to start a conversation.
t.jebel akhdar checkpoint@23.0,57.7:
The checkpoint at the foot of the Jebel Akhdar road is where the police decide who goes up the mountain, and it is a stop you cannot ignore. The road climbs from the plain at the edge of Birkat al Mouz to a plateau around two thousand metres, and it is steep, with gradients of up to about twelve per cent and hairpins carved into the rock. Because of that, for years only four-wheel-drive vehicles have been allowed through, and the rules have been enforced strictly. Whether a motorcycle may pass depends on current policy and on the officer on duty, so ask, and be ready to turn round if the answer is no.

If you do get through, the road is memorable. It climbs in tight bends up a massive cliff of grey limestone, with the plain dropping away behind you, and at the top the landscape changes. Jebel Akhdar means green mountain, and the name makes sense: terraced fields, walnut and pomegranate trees, apricots and rose bushes cover the slopes, watered by springs and a clever system of channels. The cool air at altitude, many degrees cooler than the plain, is a relief. Every spring the damask roses bloom, and the villagers distil rosewater from them, a tradition that has gone on for generations.

The rocky canyons nearby are among the deepest in Oman, and the plateau has hiking trails, abandoned villages and viewpoints. Mist can fill the valleys in the morning, and in winter, the night temperature can fall to freezing. It is a real mountain, and it deserves respect.

Izki, about fifteen kilometres away, and Nizwa, a bit farther, have all the services you need. A short stop at the checkpoint will tell you what is allowed. If you cannot go up, there is plenty to see around Birkat al Mouz, and the fort at Nizwa and its Friday market are well worth the ride. Carry your documents, since you may be asked for them, and be polite and patient. A smile and a calm tone will take you a long way in Oman.
t.al hamra@23.1,57.3:
Al Hamra is a town of old mud-brick houses at the foot of the Hajar mountains, and the pale walls and flat roofs of its old quarter blend so completely into the hillside that you can ride past without noticing them. The old town is built of mud, stone and palm trunks, and much of it is a tangle of narrow lanes and tall, windowless walls, where families lived for centuries. A few houses have been restored, and one of them is a small museum showing how people lived, with kitchens, grain stores and stables. The new town lies below, with its shops, mosque and petrol stations, and a modern road runs through it.

Water is the secret of Al Hamra, as of so many Omani villages. A falaj runs through the town, bringing water from the mountain to gardens of date palms, and the sound of running water in a dry land is a pleasure. Nearby is Misfat al Abriyeen, a village of stone houses stacked up a hillside, with narrow lanes and terraced gardens, and it is well worth a visit if you have time.

For riders, Al Hamra matters as the gateway to Jebel Shams, at about 3,000 metres the highest mountain in Oman. The road climbs from the town into the mountains in a long series of bends, with views over canyons and plateaus, and the temperature drops as you rise. The tarmac is good for much of the way, but the last section is gravel and needs care. Rain is rare, but when it comes, it can turn dry riverbeds into torrents, so stay out of wadis if the sky looks threatening. The best season is winter, from November to March, when the days are mild and the air is clear.

Al Hamra has fuel stations, shops and small restaurants, and it is the place to fill the tank and buy water before heading up. Bahla, about sixteen kilometres away, is a larger town with a famous fort, also on the UNESCO list, and has more services. Try a plate of shuwa, meat slow-cooked underground in a spiced marinade, if you can find it, or simpler dishes of rice and chicken. A cup of sweet tea in the shade of the old town is the best way to end the visit.
t.wadi ghul@23.2,57.2:
Wadi Ghul lies at the foot of Jebel Shams, where a deep canyon opens in the mountain wall, and it has the nickname of the Grand Canyon of Oman, a title the locals are happy to use even if the scale is smaller. From the rim, the cliffs fall away for about a kilometre, a vast trench of grey and ochre rock, with the dry bed of the wadi twisting at the bottom. On the canyon wall, a few abandoned villages cling to the slopes, houses of stone and mud that look like a bird's nest on a ledge. A narrow footpath, known as the Balcony Walk, follows the rim at a dizzying height, and it is a popular walk for those with a head for heights.

The road to the canyon climbs from Al Hamra in a series of bends, and the last stretch is gravel, often rough and loose, with steep sections and sharp corners. It needs a high-clearance vehicle and a steady hand, and a motorbike should be sturdy and the rider confident. The altitude brings cooler air, and in winter the nights are cold, with frost on the ground. On a clear day, the view of the canyon in the early morning, when the light rakes across the walls, is a revelation.

The Hajar mountains are old, and the rocks here include slabs of ancient sea floor pushed up and across the land, a geologists' dream. Goats and wild tahr, a rare mountain goat, live on the cliffs, though you are unlikely to see the tahr. Eagles ride the thermals above the rim, and the silence is deep. A few families still live on the plateau, keeping goats and growing a few crops, and you may meet them as you ride. They are polite and welcoming, so greet them in the traditional way, with salaam alaikum.

Al Hamra has stations, and Bahla, a bit farther away, is a larger town, with more choice. Fill the tank in Al Hamra, and carry water and food, since camps near the rim offer only basic meals. Respect the edge, as there are few barriers, and ride slowly. Do not go near the edge in wind or in the dark.
t.jebel hafit north tombs@24.2,55.8:
Jebel Hafit is the lone mountain that rises out of the desert at the edge of Al Ain, in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, and it is the highest point in the emirate at about 1,250 metres. It stands almost alone, a long, whale-backed ridge of pale limestone, with the Omani border running along its southern flank, and from the summit you can look out over a wide plain of sand, date plantations and the white buildings of the city. The geology is old and visibly folded, with fossils of shells and corals in the rock.

The slopes are also scattered with ancient beehive tombs, which give the area its place in world history. Dating back about five thousand years, to the Early Bronze Age, these round stone structures, built of stacked local rock, were used for burials, and hundreds of them dot the ridges, some in good condition. They are named the Hafit tombs after the mountain and are part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Cultural Sites of Al Ain, along with the oases and old forts. At sunset, the shapes of the stone towers against the sky are impressive.

The road up the mountain is the reason many riders come. Jebel Hafit Mountain Road runs for about twelve kilometres, with sixty or so bends, and climbs about a thousand metres to a viewing platform near the summit, with a hotel perched on a ledge. It was built with wide lanes and generous corners, the surface is smooth and well maintained, and it is regarded as one of the best driving roads in the Gulf. At weekends and in the evening, it fills with cars and motorbikes, so a weekday morning is calmer, and speed limits are enforced with cameras.

Conditions are demanding in another way, because of the heat. From May to September, daytime temperatures often exceed forty-five degrees, and riding in full gear is hard, so go at dawn or after sunset, and drink plenty of water. The cooler months, from November to March, are far more comfortable. Wind and blowing sand can reduce visibility, and a sandstorm can arise quickly.

Fuel is easy in Al Ain, with stations on all main roads, and the city has plenty of cafes and supermarkets. Al Buraimi, across the border in Oman, is only minutes away, and carrying your passport is sensible. There are no services on the mountain itself apart from the hotel and the cafes at the summit. Date palms, the old oasis and a fresh juice in town make a pleasant finish.
t.al jimi oasis@24.3,55.7:
Al Jimi is one of those places where the desert simply stops being the main character. The oasis sits in the old part of Al Ain, a city the Emiratis call the Garden City, and a few kilometres on the other side of the line lies Al Buraymi in Oman. The two towns grew up around the same underground water and the same date gardens, and for most of history nobody drew a border through them.

What makes the oasis worth a stop is the system underneath it. Water was brought down from the hills through falaj channels, narrow stone and mud conduits that run for kilometres and still feed the date palms in turn, each plot getting its share by a schedule that older families remember. Walk in under the fronds and the temperature drops by what feels like ten degrees, the air smells of damp earth and sun-warmed dates, and the noise of the road vanishes. The Al Ain oases were put on the UNESCO list in 2011 together with the Bronze Age tombs and the Hili sites, and Al Jimi is one of the easiest to visit because it is right in town.

The riding is not the point here, honestly. You arrive on wide city roads with roundabouts every few hundred metres, and the real scenery is on the horizon: the long grey ridge of Jebel Hafit, which climbs to roughly 1,240 metres and carries one of the most famous motorbike roads in the Gulf up its eastern flank, a ribbon of tight hairpins with a hotel and lookout at the top. That is the reason a rider ends up in Al Ain at all. Do the climb early, before the sun is properly up, because from May to September the afternoon heat is brutal and the tarmac gets greasy and soft.

Fuel is no issue, since Al Ain is a city of hundreds of thousands and the stations are everywhere, as they are in Al Buraymi. If you cross into Oman at any point you will need your passport, your bike papers and the right insurance, and the formalities take longer than the distance would suggest, so plan accordingly. Winter, from November to March, is the season to be here: dry, bright, mild mornings, and the oasis at its best. Stop for a coffee with dates in the shade, listen to the falaj trickle, and let the engine tick as it cools before the next climb.

Muscat is long, low and white, a city squeezed between the Gulf of Oman and the bare ridges of the Hajar mountains. Instead of towers it has a limit on building heights and a taste for cream-coloured walls, so the whole coast looks calm. The old heart is at Muttrah, where a corniche curves around a working harbour, the souq lies in a maze of alleys filled with silver, frankincense and cloth, and two sixteenth-century Portuguese forts, Jalali and Mirani, stand watch on rocks above the old palace of the sultan at Al Alam. The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, finished in 2001, is the grand modern counterpart, with a vast carpet and a chandelier that dazzles even people who say they are not impressed.

For a rider the city is a gateway. The new expressways cut inland through the mountains toward Nizwa and the interior, climbing through rocky gorges where the rock is rust, black and grey and the air feels thin and dry. Beyond, there are forts, date gardens and the high plateau of Jebel Shams. Two of the rides here are about the falaj, the ancient irrigation channels that carry water from mountain springs to villages by gravity, and the World Heritage listing for the aflaj of Oman includes Falaj Daris at Nizwa and the Al-Khatmeen channel near Birkat Al Mawz. Some of these systems are believed to be well over a thousand years old, and a village committee still divides the water by time.

The weather settles the riding season. From late October to March the days are warm and pleasant, but in summer the heat is severe, with temperatures over forty degrees, and a ride in full gear is only for dawn and dusk. Roads are excellent, with good signs in English, and speed cameras are frequent and strictly enforced. Dust and sand blow across the road in places, and camels and goats do cross, particularly at night.

Fuel is cheap and available on every main road, and in the capital you will never be far from a station, a cafe or a workshop. Try the halwa, the sticky spiced sweet that Omanis serve with coffee, and take the coffee as it comes, small and flavoured with cardamom. A visit to the harbour at sunset is worth the time.

Puerto Madryn is the base for one of the best wildlife rides in South America, and the town sits on the Golfo Nuevo, a wide blue bay on the Atlantic coast of Chubut, a flat, windy, treeless stretch of Patagonia. About sixty-five thousand people live here, enough to guarantee fuel, supermarkets, mechanics and decent restaurants. It is also the starting point for the Peninsula Valdes, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with roads leading to colonies of sea lions, elephant seals, penguins and, in season, whales.

The ride from town toward the peninsula crosses open steppe, a sea of low grey-green scrub under an enormous sky, with long straights and gentle curves. The tarmac on the main roads is good, but the real challenge is the wind, which can blow hard and unpredictably, and gravel sections on side roads require care. At the entrance to the peninsula there is a fee, and speed limits are enforced to protect wildlife, which often crosses the road. Early morning and evening bring the best light and the most animals, while midday can be hot and glaring. Be careful of guanacos and rheas on the road.

The town has a history that surprises visitors. In 1865, a group of Welsh settlers arrived on the ship Mimosa, hoping to establish a Welsh-speaking colony free of English rule, and they landed here before heading inland to the Chubut valley. Their descendants still live in the region, and in nearby towns such as Gaiman you can drink tea and eat cake in Welsh tea houses. The town is named after Love Jones-Parry, Lord Madryn, a Welsh supporter of the project, which gives a distinctly unexpected flavour to the Argentine coast.

The nature is the main attraction. From roughly June to December, southern right whales come to the sheltered bays to breed, and they can often be seen from the shore. Magellanic penguins nest at Punta Tombo, a few hours south, and sea lions and elephant seals lounge on the beaches. The air smells of salt and kelp, and the sea glitters in the sun.

Fill up in town before heading out, carry water and sun protection, and plan for strong wind. The distances are long and services are limited, but the wildlife is worth every kilometre.

The Saiq Plateau is the high, cool shelf of Jebel Akhdar, the Green Mountain, which rises to over 2,000 metres in the Hajar range of northern Oman, and it feels like another country compared with the desert below. Terraced orchards of pomegranates, apricots, walnuts and roses grow in villages perched on the mountainside, watered by ancient falaj channels, and in spring, the rose harvest fills the air with perfume. Rosewater is distilled in small stills, and the roses bloom in April. Nizwa and Izki, in the plain below, are the nearest towns, with fuel and shops.

The road up is one of the steepest paved roads in the Gulf, with gradients of up to about twenty degrees, and it is restricted to four-wheel-drive vehicles at a checkpoint at the foot, where officials check the vehicle. Motorbikes are generally not allowed, so riders need to ask about the current rules at the checkpoint, and be prepared to be turned back. The surface is smooth tarmac with hairpins, and it climbs from the dusty plain to the cool plateau in a short distance. The temperature is noticeably cooler on top, often ten degrees lower than in Nizwa.

The plateau has a long history, and it was the stronghold of the Imamate rebels in the 1950s, when British-backed forces took control after a bitter campaign. Today, the villages of Wadi Bani Habib, Al Ayn and Sayq are quiet, with old mud-brick houses, stone terraces and a few small hotels. The Diana's Point viewpoint looks over a vast canyon, and walking trails follow the old water channels along the cliffs. The Hajar mountains are old, formed from ancient sea floor, and in places, you can see folded layers of limestone.

Be prepared with fuel and water, since supplies on the plateau are limited, and the nearest pumps are in the plain below. The weather is mild in summer and cold in winter, when frost and even snow can occur. Light is best early or late, and in the evening, the sunset over the canyon is spectacular. Local food includes shuwa, slow-cooked meat, dates and Omani coffee flavoured with cardamom. Be respectful of local customs and dress modestly.
t.jebel shams viewpoint@23.2,57.2:
Jebel Shams, the Mountain of the Sun, is the highest peak in Oman, at about 3,000 metres, and the road to the viewpoint brings you to the edge of Wadi Ghul, often called the Grand Canyon of Arabia. The canyon is about a kilometre deep, with walls that drop almost vertically into a gorge of ochre and grey rock, and the abandoned village of Ghul clings to a ledge far below. The plateau is cool, with a thin atmosphere and long views, and in winter, it can be cold enough for frost. The nearest towns, Rustaq, Bahla and Bayt al Awabi, are thirty kilometres or so away on the plain.

The road from the plain is steep and winding, with a section of unpaved track near the top, so it is best tackled in daylight, in dry weather. The first stretch is smooth tarmac, with tight hairpins and views over the plain, and the last part is gravel, with loose rocks and steep gradients. Riders on road bikes may find it tricky, but those on adventure bikes should manage. There are no barriers at the viewpoint, and the edge is sharp, so take care, especially with children and in wind.

The Hajar mountains were formed when the ocean floor was pushed up over the Arabian plate, and the rocks include fossilised seabed and ancient limestone. The plateau is home to Arabian tahr, a shy mountain goat, and to birds of prey, including Bonelli's eagle and lammergeier. Juniper trees grow in the highlands, and wild herbs scent the air. A walking trail, the Balcony Walk, follows the canyon rim and an old water channel to the abandoned village of Sap Bani Khamis, an easy and spectacular walk.

Fuel and food should be taken from Bahla or Nizwa, as there are no pumps on the plateau, and only a small camp or two offers refreshment. Carry water, a warm layer and a torch if you stay for sunset, because the temperature drops fast after dark. The best time is October to April, since summer is very hot on the plain. The view, which looks out into a sea of rock, is worth the climb.

Birkat al Mawz sits at the foot of the Jebel Akhdar, where the mountains of the Hajar range rise abruptly from the gravel plains of interior Oman, and it is a classic Omani oasis: date palm groves watered by a falaj, an ancient irrigation channel, mud-brick houses, a fort, and the bare, folded mountains rising behind. The name means pool of bananas, and bananas do grow in the gardens, along with dates, limes and mangoes, all watered by the channel that brings water from the mountains.

The falaj system is one of Oman's great achievements. These channels, some of them more than a thousand years old, carry water from springs or underground sources, sometimes for many kilometres, to the villages and fields, and the water is shared among farmers according to ancient rules, measured in time shares. Five of Oman's aflaj are UNESCO World Heritage sites, including one nearby, and walking along the channels through the palm groves is a cool, peaceful experience. The fort at Birkat al Mawz, Bait al Rudaydah, has been restored and stands at the edge of the oasis.

Izki, about ten kilometres away, is one of the oldest towns in Oman, with a history going back to pre-Islamic times, and Nizwa, a little further, was the capital of Oman for centuries. Nizwa's great round fort, built in the seventeenth century, dominates the town, and the souq beside it is famous for its silver, pottery and the Friday morning livestock market, where goats and cattle are paraded and sold amid a lot of shouting and haggling.

From Birkat al Mawz, the road to Jebel Akhdar begins its climb, and there is a police checkpoint at the foot of the mountain where vehicles are checked. For years, only four-wheel-drive vehicles have been allowed to continue, because of the steep gradients, so if you are planning to ride up, ask about the rules for motorcycles before you set off. Fuel, food and supplies are available in Birkat al Mawz and Izki, and Nizwa has everything. The heat in summer is intense, with temperatures well above forty degrees, so the cooler months, from October to April, are when you want to be here.
