The road up the Jebel Akhdar is one of the steepest paved roads in the Arabian peninsula, and it does not ease you in. From the police checkpoint near Birkat al Mawz, it climbs relentlessly through a gorge and up the bare, rocky face of the mountain, gaining over a thousand metres in a short distance, with gradients that test brakes on the way down and engines on the way up. Escape lanes filled with gravel line the descent, for trucks and cars whose brakes have failed, and they tell you everything about the gradient.

The landscape is stark and dramatic: grey and brown limestone, folded and twisted into extraordinary shapes by the forces that built the Hajar mountains, with almost no vegetation apart from a few acacias and wild olive trees clinging to the rock. The geology here is famous among scientists, because the Hajar contains one of the best exposed slices of ocean crust and mantle in the world, pushed up onto the Arabian plate millions of years ago. The rocks change colour as you climb, and the views back over the plains towards Izki and Nizwa grow wider with every bend.

The mountain has a dramatic history. In the 1950s, the Jebel Akhdar was the stronghold of a rebellion against the Sultan, led by the Imam of Oman and his supporters, who held the plateau for several years. The rebellion was finally defeated in 1959, when British special forces and the Sultan's army scaled the mountain at night and took the rebels by surprise. The plateau remained a military zone for years afterwards, and it was only opened to visitors relatively recently.

For riders, the climb is a serious undertaking. The road is well paved and wide, but the gradients are extreme, and the heat can be intense in the lower sections, even in winter. There are no services on the climb, so fill up in Izki or Birkat al Mawz before you start, carry plenty of water, and check your brakes. The checkpoint at the bottom may not allow motorcycles or two-wheel-drive vehicles, so confirm the rules before you plan the ride. The best time is early morning, before the heat builds.
t.oman jebel akhdar road point 4@23.1,57.7:
On top of the Jebel Akhdar, around two thousand metres up, the air is cool and the landscape changes completely. The Saiq plateau is a high, rocky tableland cut by deep gorges, and in the villages that cling to the edges of these gorges, terraces of fruit trees and roses step down the cliffs, watered by aflaj channels. The name Jebel Akhdar means Green Mountain, and after the bare rock of the climb, the green of the terraces is a shock. In winter it can be cold enough for frost, and occasionally snow, which draws excited crowds from the lowlands.

The plateau is famous for its roses. In spring, usually around April, the terraces around villages such as Al Ayn, Al Aqr and Ash Shirayjah are pink with Damask roses, and the villagers pick them at dawn and distil them into rosewater, using traditional clay ovens and copper pots. The rosewater is used in cooking, in perfume, and in religious ceremonies, and it is sold in small bottles all over Oman. The plateau also grows pomegranates, apricots, walnuts, peaches and grapes, and the pomegranate harvest in late summer is another highlight.

The villages are built of stone and mud, perched on the edge of the gorges, and some of them have been abandoned as people moved to the towns, while others have been restored. A walking trail links several villages along the edge of the gorge, past terraces, aflaj and ruined houses, and it is one of the best short walks in Oman. A viewpoint on the edge of the plateau is known as Diana's Point, after the Princess of Wales visited it in the 1980s.

The roads on the plateau are paved and winding, with steep sections down to the villages and fine views across the gorges. Weekdays are quiet; at weekends visitors from Muscat come up to escape the heat. There are hotels and a few restaurants, and fuel is available on the plateau, but a full tank from the plains saves worry. Summer up here is mild and winter properly cold, and remember that the descent is steep and the brakes need to be in good order.
t.oman jebel shams road point 2@23.1,57.3:
Below the highest mountain in Oman, at the mouth of a great canyon, lies the village of Wadi Ghul, where the road towards Jebel Shams leaves the plains and begins to climb. An old mud-brick village crumbles on the rocky slope above the modern houses, its ruined walls the same colour as the mountain, and the wadi behind it is the start of a gorge so deep and steep that it is often called the Grand Canyon of Arabia. Jebel Shams, the Mountain of the Sun, rises above it to around three thousand metres, catching the first light each morning.

The nearby town of Al Hamra has one of the best preserved old quarters in Oman, a cluster of two- and three-storey mud-brick houses climbing the hillside above the palm groves, some of them centuries old, and a small museum in one of the houses shows how life was lived there. A short drive away, the village of Misfat al Abriyeen hangs on the side of the mountain, with narrow lanes, stone houses and terraces watered by a falaj, and it is as lovely as any village in the country.

Further south, Bahla, about sixteen kilometres away, is home to a huge mud-brick fort, one of the oldest in Oman and a UNESCO World Heritage site, surrounded by a wall that once ran for kilometres around the oasis. The town is also known for its pottery, made from local clay and fired in traditional kilns, and for its legends of jinn, the spirits said to haunt the oasis.

The road up Jebel Shams is paved for much of the way, climbing steeply in a series of hairpins, but the upper section has been gravel for years, and conditions vary, so check before you go. At the top, a path known as the Balcony Walk runs along the rim of the canyon, with drops of hundreds of metres below. The views are extraordinary. There are no services on the mountain, apart from a few simple camps and guesthouses, so fill up in Bahla or Al Hamra, carry plenty of water, and start early, before the heat of the day.
